cleanIntro: The 783 is the most thoroughly documented rifle in Remington's current catalogue — the book takes it from bolt-out field strip through barrelled action out of the stock, receiver and trigger flushed as a unit, bolt head off its pin, and a twenty-six step function test. The one thing that is genuinely different from every other bolt gun here: this bolt is serial-matched to this receiver, and the book says so in as many words.

steps.title: Safety lever fully rearward until the safety arm stops
steps.action: Find the safety on the shooter's right at the rear of the receiver and pull the lever fully to the rear toward "S" until the safety arm stops moving.
steps.prose: The 783 safety blocks the trigger outright — with it engaged the trigger will not move at all, which is the check you will make later in the function test. "Until the safety arm stops" is the operative phrase: a lever nudged most of the way back can leave the block only partly across, and there is no red band on this rifle to tell you at a glance. It does not lock the bolt handle, so you can and should open the action and unload with it still engaged.
steps.quote: The safety mechanism is located on the shooters right towards the rear of the receiver. To engage the safety mechanism, pull the safety lever fully to the rear toward the “S” position until the safety arm stops. See Picture 4.
steps.cite: Owner's Manual — Instruction Book For: Model 783™ Bolt Action Rifles — 304392 Rev. 0426 — Important Parts of the Firearm — The Safety Mechanism, p.8

steps.title: This bolt belongs to this receiver — check the last three digits
steps.action: Before anything comes apart, read the last three digits stamped on the bolt and check them against the receiver's serial number on the left of the receiver.
steps.prose: The 783 uses a two-piece striker bolt whose head is fitted to hold correct headspace on the rifle it was built with, which is why Remington marks it with the last three digits of the receiver serial and tells you to keep the pair together. This matters most on a bench with two 783s on it, or after a deep clean where two bolts have been apart at once — a swapped bolt is not a fit-and-finish problem, it is a headspace problem. Note the number now, while both parts are still assembled and there is no doubt which belongs to which.
steps.quote: The bolt assemblies are not interchangeable between rifles.
steps.cite: Owner's Manual — Instruction Book For: Model 783™ Bolt Action Rifles — 304392 Rev. 0426 — Important Parts of the Firearm — The Bolt Assembly, p.9
steps.warn: Remington: only use the original bolt assembly within your firearm; use of an improper bolt and receiver combination may cause property damage, personal injury and/or death.

steps.title: Magazine box out, bolt back, eyes into the ejection port
steps.action: Press the magazine latch release and draw the detachable magazine box out of the well, raise the bolt handle, pull the bolt fully rearward, and look into the ejection port to confirm both chamber and magazine well are empty.
steps.prose: The 783 feeds from a detachable box, so the magazine comes out first and takes the whole magazine problem with it — but the chamber is a separate question and the box coming out proves nothing about it. Pull the bolt fully back, not part way, so the extractor has actually dragged whatever was in the chamber clear and you are looking at bare chamber wall. Do this by eye and then by finger, because a brass case rim in a shadowed port reads as nothing at all.
steps.quote: 4. Open the action by raising the bolt handle. 5. Pull the bolt fully rearward. 6. Look into the ejection port, visually check the chamber and magazine to make sure the firearm is completely unloaded.
steps.cite: Owner's Manual — Instruction Book For: Model 783™ Bolt Action Rifles — 304392 Rev. 0426 — The Barrel — To Check the Barrel for Obstructions, steps 4-6, p.11

steps.title: Bolt release button in, bolt straight out the back
steps.action: With the action open, push the bolt release button and slide the bolt assembly rearward and out of the receiver.
steps.prose: The bolt release on a 783 is a button on the left rear of the receiver, not a lever inside the trigger guard as on a 700 — press it and hold it while the bolt travels the last of its stroke, and the bolt lifts straight out. If the bolt stops dead at the same point every time, you are letting go of the button too early rather than fighting a burr. Catch the bolt as it clears; the plastic bolt shroud at the rear cracks if it lands on a hard bench.
steps.quote: 5. Disengage the bolt stop by pushing the bolt release button while sliding the bolt assembly rearward until it is clear of the receiver. See Picture 10.
steps.cite: Owner's Manual — Instruction Book For: Model 783™ Bolt Action Rifles — 304392 Rev. 0426 — To Remove the Bolt Assembly, step 5, p.10

steps.title: Look through from the chamber end, then clean the same way
steps.action: With the bolt out and the magazine out, sight through the receiver and barrel from the chamber end to check for an obstruction, and run every patch and brush in that same direction.
steps.prose: A 783's button-rifled barrel is threaded into the receiver rather than pinned, and the crown at the muzzle is what your groups live on — a rod pushed in from the muzzle bears on it every stroke. Working from the chamber also carries fouling out of the bore instead of into the locking lug recesses. Remington's own bore sequence starts with a Brite Bore-soaked patch to lift the loose residue before any brush touches the rifling, which is worth following in order rather than reaching straight for the brush.
steps.quote: 8. To check for an obstruction look through the receiver and barrel from the chamber end.
steps.cite: Owner's Manual — Instruction Book For: Model 783™ Bolt Action Rifles — 304392 Rev. 0426 — The Barrel — To Check the Barrel for Obstructions, step 8, p.11
steps.warn: Remington: NEVER try to remove an object from the barrel by loading another cartridge and firing.

steps.title: Field strip complete
steps.action: Magazine box out, bolt assembly out, chamber empty, safety at "S". That is the whole field strip — the stock, the barrelled action and the trigger stay together.
steps.prose: From here you can clean the bore from the chamber, the bolt face and extractor, and the visible part of the raceways, which covers a normal range session. The deeper procedure the book prints — two takedown screws out, barrelled action lifted from the stock, receiver and trigger flushed with action cleaner, bolt head off its pin — is the Deep Clean branch, and it is bounded: Remington states plainly that the rifle is not taken further apart than the manual describes.
steps.quote: Note: The Model 783™ firearms should NOT be disassembled beyond what is described in this manual, except by the factory or a Remington Authorized Repair Center.
steps.cite: Owner's Manual — Instruction Book For: Model 783™ Bolt Action Rifles — 304392 Rev. 0426 — To Disassemble and Clean the Firearm — opening note, p.17

deepSteps.title: Two takedown screws, 9/64" Allen, barrelled action out of the stock
deepSteps.action: With magazine and bolt already out, back out the front and rear takedown screws with a 9/64" Allen wrench and lift the barrelled action clear of the stock.
deepSteps.prose: Both screws thread up into the receiver through the stock's bedding blocks; slacken them alternately a couple of turns at a time so the action is never held on one fastener while the other is loose. The front screw sits ahead of the magazine well, the rear behind the trigger — they are not the same length and they get retorqued to different figures on the way back, so keep them identified. Lift the action straight up rather than rocking it out; the recoil lug is a close fit in its slot and levering it wears the bedding.
deepSteps.quote: 7. Remove the barred/action from the stock by removing the two takedown screws (front & rear), using a 9/64” Allen Wrench. See Picture 17.
deepSteps.cite: Owner's Manual — Instruction Book For: Model 783™ Bolt Action Rifles — 304392 Rev. 0426 — To Disassemble and Clean the Firearm, step 7, p.17

deepSteps.title: Flush the whole inside of the receiver, then dry it properly
deepSteps.action: Spray and brush every component inside the receiver with Rem Action Cleaner, then dry it fully with compressed air or by standing it to air-dry, and finish with a light application of Rem Oil inside and out.
deepSteps.prose: With the stock off you have access to the underside of the receiver and the magazine well, which is where powder residue and dust actually collect on a 783 — the ejection port only ever shows you the top half of the problem. Action cleaner flashes off fast; the point of drying before oiling is that any left behind will thin the oil you put on top of it. Keep the spray out of the muzzle end and keep the rifle tilted so it drains forward and out rather than back into the stock inletting.
deepSteps.quote: 9. Thoroughly spray and brush all components inside the receiver using RemTM Action Cleaner.
deepSteps.cite: Owner's Manual — Instruction Book For: Model 783™ Bolt Action Rifles — 304392 Rev. 0426 — To Clean the Receiver, step 9, p.17

deepSteps.title: The trigger assembly is cleaned in place, never taken off
deepSteps.action: Leave the trigger assembly on the receiver and clean and lubricate the two as one unit — spray Rem Action Cleaner into the four points marked in the manual's Picture 18.
deepSteps.prose: The 783's trigger is a factory-set unit with a blade-style trigger release in the face of the trigger, and the release timing is part of what the function test checks — taking the housing off the receiver disturbs exactly the relationships you have no way of resetting. Four points, sprayed until the solvent runs clear, then worked, then sprayed again and dried, then one drop of oil at each of the same four. One drop means one drop; a flooded 783 trigger collects lint and goes sluggish in cold weather.
deepSteps.quote: NOTE: Clean and lubricate the receiver and trigger assemblies as a unit. Do not remove the trigger assembly from the receiver.
deepSteps.cite: Owner's Manual — Instruction Book For: Model 783™ Bolt Action Rifles — 304392 Rev. 0426 — To Clean and Lubricate the Trigger Assembly — note before step 12, p.17
deepSteps.warn: Remington: all repairs to the trigger assembly must be made by the factory or a Remington Authorized Repair Center.

deepSteps.title: Hold the trigger back and cycle the sear with a punch
deepSteps.action: With the safety in the "FIRE" position, pull and hold the trigger rearward, depress the sear with a small punch or screwdriver at lubrication point 1, and release it several times.
deepSteps.prose: This is what actually moves solvent through the engagement surfaces rather than merely wetting them — the sear only exposes its bearing face when the trigger is held back and the sear is pushed down. Use a punch that fits the sear rather than a wide blade that can skate off onto the engagement edge. Watch the return each time: the sear must come back up to its full height with no hesitation, and if it does not, that is the finding, not an excuse for another spray.
deepSteps.quote: 14. Pull and hold the trigger rearward. While using a small punch or screwdriver, depress the sear (Lubrication Point 1, see Picture 18) and release multiple times. See Picture 19.
deepSteps.cite: Owner's Manual — Instruction Book For: Model 783™ Bolt Action Rifles — 304392 Rev. 0426 — To Clean and Lubricate the Trigger Assembly, step 14, p.17
deepSteps.warn: Remington: if the sear does not return to the full upward position without hesitation, the firearm is NOT in a safe operating condition and must not be used until repaired by a Remington Authorized Repair Center.

deepSteps.title: Bolt plug and firing pin an eighth of a turn clockwise
deepSteps.action: Compress the firing pin spring by hand, or with pliers across the firing pin head and bolt plug, then rotate the bolt plug and firing pin assembly clockwise one eighth of a turn and pull the bolt plug outward to draw the firing pin assembly out of the bolt body.
deepSteps.prose: The eighth-turn is a bayonet release, not a thread — it only lets go while the spring is compressed, which is why the compression comes first and why letting go part way lets the assembly snap back under load. If you use pliers, pad the jaws: the 783 bolt plug is a soft finished part and it will carry the tooth marks forever. Keep the muzzle end of the bolt pointed away from your face while the spring is under compression.
deepSteps.caution: Remington's wording for the pliers: be sure to take precautions not to mar the bolt plug.
deepSteps.quote: 2. Rotate the bolt plug and firing pin assembly clockwise 1/8th of a turn. See Picture 21.
deepSteps.cite: Owner's Manual — Instruction Book For: Model 783™ Bolt Action Rifles — 304392 Rev. 0426 — To Disassemble the Bolt Assembly, step 2, p.18

deepSteps.title: Drift the bolt head pin and take the head off the body
deepSteps.action: With the firing pin assembly out, push the bolt head pin out with a punch and remove the bolt head and the bolt friction washer from the bolt body.
deepSteps.prose: This is the step that makes the 783 bolt a two-piece assembly, and it is also the one that can leave the rifle unsafe if you get careless — the head, the friction washer and the pin all belong to this bolt and this receiver, so nothing goes into a communal parts tray. Support the bolt body in a block while you drift the pin rather than hammering it against a hard bench top. Note the washer's position on the bolt head shaft before it comes off; it goes back on the shaft before the head goes into the body.
deepSteps.quote: 4. Remove the bolt head and the bolt friction washer from the bolt body by removing the bolt head pin with a punch. See Picture 22.
deepSteps.cite: Owner's Manual — Instruction Book For: Model 783™ Bolt Action Rifles — 304392 Rev. 0426 — To Disassemble the Bolt Assembly, step 4, p.18
deepSteps.warn: Remington: when the bolt head pin is NOT installed in the bolt assembly, the firearm is NOT safe to use.

deepSteps.title: Firing pin assembly gets cleaned whole and never opened
deepSteps.action: Spray, flush and brush all the bolt components including the firing pin assembly with Rem Action Cleaner, dry them, and apply a light coat of Rem Oil — but do not take the firing pin assembly apart.
deepSteps.prose: The firing pin, its spring and the cocking piece are a captive stack in the 783 and the book treats them as one part on purpose; there is nothing inside it the owner sets. Flush it end to end and blow it dry — residue left inside a firing pin assembly is what turns into a slow lock time and then into misfires in cold weather. Grease is allowed in exactly one place on this bolt: the cocking notch, and only if you want it there.
deepSteps.quote: Caution! Clean the firing pin assembly as a unit. Do not disassemble.
deepSteps.cite: Owner's Manual — Instruction Book For: Model 783™ Bolt Action Rifles — 304392 Rev. 0426 — To Clean the Bolt and the Firing Pin Assemblies — caution, p.18

deepSteps.title: Bolt handle 180 degrees from the ejector on reassembly
deepSteps.action: Slide the friction washer onto the bolt head shaft, push the head into the bolt body oriented with the bolt handle 180 degrees from the ejector as viewed from the front, then line the bolt head pin holes up and drive the pin home.
deepSteps.prose: Orientation is the whole trick here — the head will physically enter the body at more than one clock position, but only one puts the ejector opposite the handle, and only in that one do the pin holes line up. Sight down the front of the bolt to set it rather than eyeballing from the side. Once the pin is through, confirm it sits flush on both sides and that the head still has its slight float in the body; a head that has gone in rigid means the washer is misplaced.
deepSteps.aside: Before the bolt goes back in the rifle the firing pin assembly must be cocked, with the cocking arm sitting in the small cocked notch (p.9, Picture 8).
deepSteps.quote: Orient the bolt handle 180 degrees from the ejector, as viewed from the front.
deepSteps.cite: Owner's Manual — Instruction Book For: Model 783™ Bolt Action Rifles — 304392 Rev. 0426 — To Reassemble Bolt Assembly, step 2, p.19

cleaning.name: BORE & CHAMBER
tasks: Brite Bore-soaked patch on a jag first, chamber end to muzzle, several passes to lift the loose residue
Then the correct-calibre brush, sprayed with Brite Bore, several passes — always chamber to muzzle
Patch, brush, patch again with a fresh patch each time until one comes out with no fouling residue on it
Rem Oil patch through, then a dry patch behind it to take the excess out of the chamber
Light Rem Oil on the outside of the barrel with a soft cloth

cleaning.name: BOLT ASSEMBLY
tasks: Bolt face, extractor cut and ejector plunger sprayed, flushed and brushed with Rem Action Cleaner
Firing pin assembly cleaned as a unit — never opened up
Air dry or blow dry every component before any oil goes near it
Light Rem Oil on all bolt surfaces; grease on the cocking notch only if wanted
Confirm the last three serial digits on the bolt still match the receiver before it goes back

cleaning.name: RECEIVER, TRIGGER & MAGAZINE (deep only)
tasks: Receiver sprayed and brushed inside with Rem Action Cleaner, dried, then lightly oiled inside and out
Trigger assembly flushed at the four points of Picture 18, worked with trigger and sear, flushed again and dried
One drop of Rem Oil at each of the four trigger points, then a light external spray and the excess wiped off
Magazine components flushed and dried; on a .223 or .222 rifle the synthetic magazine insert stays in place
Follower checked to move freely in the housing before the magazine goes back in the rifle

reassembly: Barrelled action into the stock with the bolt and magazine still out.
Takedown screws in clockwise with a 9/64" Allen wrench and torqued: front screw 30 to 35 inch pounds, rear screw 20 to 25 inch pounds.
Confirm the barrel is free of obstructions before the bolt goes anywhere near the receiver.
Firing pin assembly cocked — cocking arm in the small cocked notch — then bolt lugs aligned with the receiver cuts and the bolt pushed forward until the bolt stop engages.
Verify the bolt head pin is present. If it is missing the rifle is not safe and does not get used.
Magazine box pushed into the well until the latch fully engages.
Safety back to "S", then run the function test before the rifle is loaded.
fncheck: Remington prints a full function test for the 783 and it is worth running as printed. Unloaded, magazine out: with the safety engaged, pull the trigger — the firing pin must NOT release. Move the safety to "F" and pull again — the striker must release, and the trigger must return completely forward every time it is let go. Then, still in "FIRE", pull the trigger WITHOUT touching the blade trigger release in the middle of it — the striker must not release. Finally, with an empty magazine latched in, close the action smartly: the striker must stay cocked and the magazine must stay latched. Any failure means the rifle is not fired — it goes to a Remington Authorized Repair Center.
